title: 2 Chronicles 25:1–13
context: Amaziah son of Joash reigns twenty-nine years. He does right, "but not with a perfect heart." He executes his father's assassins but spares their children according to the law of Moses. Preparing to fight Edom, he hires a hundred thousand men from Israel, but a man of God warns him to send them home, and he obeys at the cost of the silver. He defeats Seir in the Valley of Salt, and his dismissed Israelite mercenaries raid the cities of Judah. This parallels 2 Kings 14:1–7, which is much shorter and does not record the hired army or the events of verses 12–13.

verses.text: Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jehoaddan, of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Amaziah begins to reign at twenty-five and reigns twenty-nine years; his mother is Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that he comes to the throne after his father's violent death, with an opportunity to choose a better path.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:2. The regnal formula situates Amaziah within the line of David that God continues to preserve despite the failures of its kings.

verses.text: He did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, but not with a perfect heart.
verses.arminianNotes: He does right "but not with a perfect heart." Arminian readers note that outward obedience without wholehearted devotion leaves a person vulnerable, as Amaziah's later choices will show.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 14:3 says "yet not like David his father." The Chronicler's phrase about the heart explains the inner cause of the divided loyalty that later becomes open idolatry.

verses.text: Now when the kingdom was established to him, he killed his servants who had killed his father the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Once established, Amaziah kills the servants who killed his father. Arminian readers note that he brings justice against those who murdered the king, an act of responsible rule.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:5. The king waits until his kingdom is secure, then deals with the conspirators who had shed royal blood.

verses.text: But he didn’t put their children to death, but did according to that which is written in the law in the book of Moses, as the LORD commanded, saying, “The fathers shall not die for the children, neither shall the children die for the fathers; but every man shall die for his own sin.”
verses.arminianNotes: He spares their children, following the law: "every man shall die for his own sin." Arminian readers see personal accountability before God affirmed, consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 14:6.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the quoted law corresponds to Deuteronomy 24:16. God's law restrains royal vengeance, and Amaziah's obedience here is commended.

verses.text: Moreover Amaziah gathered Judah together and ordered them according to their fathers’ houses, under captains of thousands and captains of hundreds, even all Judah and Benjamin. He counted them from twenty years old and upward, and found that there were three hundred thousand chosen men, able to go out to war, who could handle spear and shield.
verses.arminianNotes: Amaziah musters Judah and Benjamin and finds three hundred thousand chosen men. Arminian readers note the careful preparation for war, a king exercising responsible leadership over his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this muster is recorded only in Chronicles. The size of the army sets up the question of whether Amaziah will trust in numbers or in God.

verses.text: He also hired one hundred thousand mighty men of valor out of Israel for one hundred talents of silver.
verses.arminianNotes: He hires a hundred thousand men from Israel for a hundred talents of silver. Arminian readers note that Amaziah chooses to add mercenaries from the northern kingdom, seeking strength in numbers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Israel at this time is under the house of Jehu and its continuing sins. Joining with them raises the question of alliance with those the LORD is not with.

verses.text: A man of God came to him, saying, “O king, don’t let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel, with all the children of Ephraim.
verses.arminianNotes: A man of God warns, "Don't let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel." Arminian readers see God giving Amaziah a clear choice with clear consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the warning concerns alliance with a people in persistent apostasy. Victory depends on the LORD's presence, not on the size of the coalition.

verses.text: But if you will go, take action, and be strong for the battle. God will overthrow you before the enemy; for God has power to help, and to overthrow.”
verses.arminianNotes: "God has power to help, and to overthrow." Arminian readers note that the outcome of the battle depends on Amaziah's response to God's word, not on his military strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the prophet's words confess God's sovereign power over battle. Human strength cannot secure what God does not give, and cannot prevent what he determines.

verses.text: Amaziah said to the man of God, “But what shall we do for the hundred talents which I have given to the army of Israel?” The man of God answered, “The LORD is able to give you much more than this.”
verses.arminianNotes: Amaziah asks about the hundred talents; the man of God answers, "The LORD is able to give you much more than this." Arminian readers see a test of whether Amaziah will trust God over his investment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the prophet's answer points Amaziah to God's sufficiency. Obedience may cost something, but the LORD is not limited in what he can give.

verses.text: Then Amaziah separated them, the army that had come to him out of Ephraim, to go home again. Therefore their anger was greatly kindled against Judah, and they returned home in fierce anger.
verses.arminianNotes: Amaziah sends the Israelite troops home, and they return in fierce anger. Arminian readers see real obedience at real cost, a choice to follow God's word despite the loss and the risk.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that obedience does not remove every consequence; the dismissed army's anger will soon fall on Judah. Faithfulness can bring hardship as well as blessing.

verses.text: Amaziah took courage, and led his people out and went to the Valley of Salt, and struck ten thousand of the children of Seir.
verses.arminianNotes: Amaziah takes courage, goes to the Valley of Salt, and strikes ten thousand of Seir. Arminian readers note that the victory follows his obedience, showing God's help when his word is followed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:7, which adds the taking of Sela. God grants the victory the prophet's word implied, without the hired army.

verses.text: The children of Judah carried away ten thousand alive, and brought them to the top of the rock, and threw them down from the top of the rock, so that they all were broken in pieces.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah carries away ten thousand alive, and "threw them down from the top of the rock, so that they all were broken in pieces." Arminian readers let the text's own words stand as a sober record of the war's brutality.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the verse as stated, without elaboration. This detail is not in 2 Kings 14, and the narrator records it without comment or approval.

verses.text: But the men of the army whom Amaziah sent back, that they should not go with him to battle, fell on the cities of Judah from Samaria even to Beth Horon, and struck of them three thousand, and took much plunder.
verses.arminianNotes: The dismissed Israelite army raids Judah's cities from Samaria to Beth Horon, killing three thousand. Arminian readers note that the anger of verse 10 now turns to violence against Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this episode is recorded only in Chronicles. Amaziah's earlier decision to hire the army brings painful consequences even after he obeyed the command to dismiss it.
